name: Scalp microneedling roller
lead: A scalp microneedling roller, also called a derma roller, is a handheld barrel covered in short needles that is rolled across the scalp to make many tiny punctures. People with thinning hair use it, usually alongside topical minoxidil, hoping to thicken hair and improve scalp coverage and hairline density.[1][2]

Microneedling in general, also called collagen induction therapy, skin needling or dermarolling, is a cosmetic procedure that repeatedly punctures the skin with small sterile needles; it has been used for scarring and acne, and some studies have found it paired with minoxidil more effective than minoxidil alone for androgenetic alopecia.[2] The appearance chain proponents describe is micro-injury, then a wound-healing response and better delivery of topical drugs, then more or thicker hairs in thinning areas, and a denser-looking head of hair. Consumer rollers are sold with needle lengths of roughly 0.25 to 1.0 mm.

The main published support is a 2013 randomized, evaluator-blinded pilot study from India in 100 men, which reported a larger hair-count increase at 12 weeks when weekly microneedling was added to 5% minoxidil than with minoxidil alone.[1] That study tested clinician-applied treatment with a 1.5 mm roller in a clinic, and no published trial of low-cost home rollers is available.[1][5]

paras: The device is a small roller fitted with fine needles. Rolling it over skin creates microscopic channels, a procedure known as microneedling or collagen induction therapy.[2] The Wikipedia article distinguishes this cosmetic use from microneedling used for transdermal drug delivery or vaccination.[2] In hair loss, the technique is used together with topical drugs, most often minoxidil.[1]
Consumer rollers are offered at roughly $10 to $30 and in shorter needle lengths than the instrument used in the trial; microneedling pens and clinic devices are variants of the same idea.

The authors of the 2013 pilot study propose that microneedling triggers a wound-healing response that releases platelet-derived and epidermal growth factors, activates stem cells in the follicle bulge, and upregulates genes including VEGF, beta-catenin, Wnt3a and Wnt10b; they note these ideas draw largely on mouse studies.[5] Proponents also suggest that the channels may increase absorption of topical drugs such as minoxidil.[1] How far these effects occur with the shallow needles of home devices has not been tested in published trials.

Microneedling is sometimes combined in clinics with platelet-rich plasma, made from the patient's own blood; Wikipedia says the efficacy of that combination remains in question pending scientific studies.[2] Wikipedia also cites a 2015 review of microneedling in skin of colour, a topic distinct from scalp use.[2]

The 2013 pilot enrolled 100 men aged 20 to 35 with mild to moderate androgenetic alopecia (Norwood-Hamilton grade III vertex or IV) and allocated them by coin toss to weekly microneedling plus twice-daily 5% minoxidil or to minoxidil alone for 12 weeks; 94 completed.[5] The microneedling group received a weekly session with a 1.5 mm dermaroller until mild redness appeared, and minoxidil was skipped on procedure days.[5]

Mean hair count in a fixed 1 cm2 vertex area rose by about 91 in the microneedling group versus about 22 in the minoxidil-only group (P = 0.039). Blinded reviewers rated global photographs on a 7-point scale and scored 40 microneedling patients at +2 to +3 and none of the minoxidil patients; 82 percent of the microneedling group (41 of 50) reported more than 50 percent improvement compared with 4.5 percent (2 of 44) in the other group.[5] The authors observed visible regrowth earlier in the microneedling group and reported no significant adverse effects.[5]

The authors described the work as a pilot. Limitations visible in the report include a single centre, short follow-up, no sham procedure, men only, and unresolved questions about needle size, frequency and endpoint, which the authors acknowledge.[5] No published trial has tested a consumer-grade roller used by patients at home.

Because the technique breaks the skin, irritation, bleeding and infection are possible, particularly if a roller is not cleaned or is shared between people. Wikipedia notes that infection is the main concern with microneedling in non-medical settings, citing a 2024 CDC report of three HIV diagnoses among patients of one New Mexico spa offering PRP microneedling facials, a clinical setting that differs from scalp rolling at home.[2] The pilot trial reported no significant adverse effects, and published data on adverse events from home use are limited.[5]

Threads on Hair Loss Talk and the archived r/tressless community discuss dermarolling and minoxidil results and ask whether to add a roller to a regrowth routine.[3][4] The thread titles themselves reflect the framing: results are reported as a minoxidil add-on, and newcomers ask whether the roller is worth including in a routine.

timeline.event: Randomized pilot study reports greater hair-count gain with microneedling plus minoxidil than minoxidil alone.[1]
CDC reports HIV diagnoses linked to a spa offering PRP microneedling facials; the case is cited as an infection-control warning for the technique.[2]

lore.intro: Dermarolling is discussed in hair-loss forums as an add-on to minoxidil, with threads sharing before-and-after results and asking whether to add it [3][4].

claims.believers: Users post results threads describing improvement from dermarolling with minoxidil and ask others whether to add it to a routine [3][4].
claims.experts: A 2013 pilot trial reported more hair regrowth with clinic microneedling plus minoxidil than minoxidil alone, but it was small, short and used clinician-applied treatment [1].

claims.claim: A cheap home roller works like the clinic treatment
claims.believers: Forum participants discuss home rollers as an affordable way to copy the trial protocol [3].
claims.experts: No published trial has tested home-use rollers, and the cited trial used different conditions [1].

angle.text: Users roll the device over thinning scalp areas, typically with minoxidil, to try to increase hair count and improve visible density. In the one randomized pilot trial, clinic microneedling plus minoxidil produced a larger hair-count rise than minoxidil alone.
